caption:
Your dog didn't become scared of crackers overnight, and she won't get over them overnight either.

Dussehra is the only noise night on the calendar that comes with a start time. Ravan dahan happens at an announced muhurat, in a known spot in your neighbourhood, so find out when yours is. Diwali gives no such warning. It arrives from five directions, for five days.

Which makes tonight a rehearsal. You aren't fixing anything this evening. You're finding out which dog you have: the one who startles and settles, or the one who doesn't come out. Then you have nineteen days.

The number that changed how we think about this: in a study of 1,225 dogs (PLOS One, 2019), 39% of the firework-fearful ones got better over time, 11% a great deal and 28% somewhat. The same study found 26.5% got worse, 18% slightly and 8.5% a lot. Both halves are true and both say the same thing. Noise fear is not a fixed trait of your dog. It moves, and what happens in the quiet days in between is part of which way.

Then there's the cat. In a Dutch survey of more than 3,600 dogs and cats, people reported fireworks fear in 76.8% of cats and 77.4% of dogs, the same rate. More of the cats had gone missing afterwards, 8.4% against 5.4%. But their people asked anyone for help less than half as often, 23.2% against 53.6%. Nobody told them there was anything to ask. For a cat, these nineteen days are about a room to disappear into, not a sound plan.

Two PawVeda Academy modules walk through exactly this: Diwali fireworks calm, and Diwali safe room for cats. Both are in the beta build.

One limit, out loud: if your pet panics rather than startles, a sound routine is not the answer on its own, and a vet has options worth asking about. PawVeda helps you decide when to see a vet — it doesn't replace one. Make that call in the next two weeks, not at 10pm on the 8th.

Every figure here is from European research. No Indian prevalence study turned up, and we aren't going to invent one. Photos are AI-generated.

Save it. You'll want it on the 7th.

caption:
Kishmish in the kheer, in the halwa, in the box of mithai on the table. It's a grape, dried.

Grapes and raisins can cause sudden kidney injury in some dogs. Two things make that awkward. Nobody can predict which dogs react, and no toxic dose has been established, so nobody can give you a safe number. Some dogs eat them and are fine. Some end up with kidney injury. Nobody can tell you in advance which kind yours is, and looking fine for a few hours isn't the all-clear.

So we'd give him none. And if he's already had some, call your vet now instead of waiting to see. The first sign is usually vomiting, within a day, and the sources are clear that waiting for it is the wrong order.

PawVeda helps you decide when to see a vet. It doesn't replace one.

caption:
A wet nose tells you he has a wet nose. Vets check something else.

Nose temperature and moisture aren't a good guide to overall health. Plenty of healthy dogs have dry noses, and a sick dog's nose can be as cool and wet as ever. (A nose that cracks, runs or changes is its own reason to ask a vet.) One of the first things a vet does look at is the gums: their colour, and how fast the colour comes back after a press.

Pale or white, blue, grey or purple, very red, or yellow: a gum colour that isn't his usual pink is a reason to go to a vet now, not in the morning. If the pink takes longer than two seconds to come back after a press, call your vet as well. (Merck also lists a refill faster than one second as abnormal. At home that's too fast to time, which is one reason this is a rough check.)

Do this only with a calm dog. One who is in pain or fighting for breath may bite, however gentle he usually is. And pink gums don't clear a dog who seems wrong.

PawVeda helps you decide when to see a vet. It doesn't replace one.

Look tonight, while he's fine. That's how you'll know his pink.

caption:
Every Diwali post is about dogs. Your cat noticed.

She won't come to you when the crackers start. She'll go under something: the bed, the sofa, the back of a cupboard. That isn't the plan failing. Hiding is what an anxious cat does, and Cats Protection's advice is to let her.

So give her the place now, while it's quiet. A cardboard box with a blanket, in a quiet room. Keep windows and doors shut on the night. And don't pull her out to cuddle her: picking up a frightened cat can make her more scared.

In a Dutch survey of more than 3,600 dogs and cats, pet parents reported fireworks fear in 76.8% of cats and 77.4% of dogs, and cat parents asked anyone for help less than half as often. PawVeda Academy has a module written for this: Diwali safe room for cats. It's in the beta.

caption:
“She'll eat when she's hungry.” For a cat, that wait has a clock on it, and it's a short one.

Cornell's Feline Health Center says going without food can seriously affect an adult cat in as little as 24 hours. For a kitten under six weeks, 12 hours. That isn't a day to wait out: Cornell's line is that a cat who isn't eating deserves a full veterinary workup. International Cat Care puts the difference plainly. Dogs can cope with less food for a short time, and cats need to be seen quickly. Eating much less than usual counts, not only eating nothing.

Not eating is a sign that something else is going on, so the reason to go early is to find out what. Please don't push food into her mouth. The same sources warn against it.

PawVeda helps you decide when to see a vet. It doesn't replace one. If she's off her food right now, a vet is the right call.

Save it for the day she turns away from the bowl.

caption:
If the carrier only ever appears before a vet visit, she has learned exactly what it means, and she is right.

The way out is dull: make the carrier furniture. Leave it out where she already sleeps, door open, her own blanket inside. Treats near it, then in it, and she's free to walk out. Only when she's resting in there by choice does the door close, for a few seconds at first. Then a lift. Then short drives that end back home.

It takes days for some cats and weeks for others, longer if she already has bad memories of it. Go at her pace and never push her in; that teaches the opposite lesson. In one small trial (22 cats, six weeks of reward-based carrier training) the trained cats showed less stress on the drive and needed a shorter exam at the other end.

A carrier that opens at the top, or whose top half lifts off, makes the vet's job gentler too. Cover it with a towel on the way.

PawVeda Academy runs on the same rules: rewards only, never force, and the reason behind every step. 21 illustrated modules, 11 of them for cats.

Start a few weeks before her next vet visit.

Sources: Cat Friendly Homes; International Cat Care; RSPCA Australia; Pratsch et al., Applied Animal Behaviour Science, 2018. Photo is AI-generated.

Plain roti isn't the problem. The pyaaz paratha is.

Every answer about dogs and roti is about dogs in general. Plain wheat roti, a small piece now and then, is filler: no harm for most dogs, no nutrition their food doesn't already give them. Ghee or butter on top adds fat they don't need, so go easy.

Onion and garlic are the line. Raw, cooked, or as powder in the masala, they damage red blood cells, and the signs usually show up days later, after everyone's decided he was fine. Cats are even more sensitive to onion than dogs. If he's had a pyaaz or lehsun paratha, call your vet today.

And some dogs shouldn't have the roti at all. Of 297 dogs with a confirmed food allergy, wheat was a trigger for 13% of them. So the real question is never "can dogs eat roti". It's "can this dog eat this roti". PawVeda answers against your pet's own record, so Bruno and Coco get different answers to the same question.

PawVeda helps you decide when to see a vet. It doesn't replace one.

caption:
He'll walk past a full steel bowl at home and drink from the first puddle on the road. It's only rainwater, except it has been sitting on a road he shares with rats.

Leptospirosis is a bacterial infection spread through the urine of infected animals, rodents above all, and the bacteria can survive in standing water and wet soil for weeks. Cornell's vet school says the most common way dogs catch it is water contaminated with urine: puddles, ponds, anything stagnant. It gets in through the mouth, the eyes, the nose or a cut on a paw, so wading counts as well as drinking. In a Chennai study of 210 dogs that vets already suspected of having it, the monsoon months, rodents, and wet soil or stagnant water all showed up as risk factors.

The early signs look like a lot of other things: off food, tired, vomiting, fever, a change in how much he drinks and pees. You can't rule it in or out at home, which is the point of asking early.

There is a vaccine, given every year after a two-dose start. It doesn't cover every strain, so a vaccinated dog still shouldn't drink from the road. It's worth one question at the next visit: is his leptospirosis shot current?

PawVeda helps you decide when to see a vet. It doesn't replace one. If he's off his food, tired or vomiting after a wet week, a vet is the right call.

Carry water on the walk.

caption:
Thoda dahi to chalta hai. Probably. But has anyone in the family ever said where they heard it?

Somebody did check. A team at the Indian Veterinary Research Institute in Izatnagar gave one group of Labradors traditionally set dahi every day for eight weeks, and compared them with a group that got none. Eight dogs in all. That is the entire study, and we'd rather say so first.

In those dogs, faecal pH and ammonia went down, lactobacilli and bifidobacteria went up, coliforms went down, and calcium digestibility went up. Those are measurements in eight Labradors. They aren't a promise about your dog. The study fed 100 ml a day. That is what those Labradors got in a trial, and it isn't a serving suggestion.

So: depends. On the dahi, because what was tested was dahi set the traditional way. Mishti doi and flavoured tubs weren't. And on the dog. PawVeda is built so that every answer is conditioned on your own pet's record, allergies and conditions included. Same food, different pet, different answer.

If dahi upsets his stomach, that's one for your vet. PawVeda helps you decide when to see a vet. It doesn't replace one.

Save it for the next time someone says thoda dahi de do.

Everyone's telling you to calm your dog down on Diwali. Nobody's telling you she might not be there to calm.

On Diwali night the front door opens again and again. ThePrint reported Delhi-NCR street dogs found 20 to 30 km from home after Diwali. And in a Dutch survey of more than 3,600 dogs and cats, pet parents reported more cats than dogs going missing after fireworks, 8.4% against 5.4%.

The morning after Diwali, the lane is full of spent crackers. Walk it before she does.

Fireworks contain potassium nitrate, sulphur and heavy-metal colourants. Eaten, they can cause vomiting, belly pain and worse (Pet Poison Helpline). If she's eaten one, call your vet, and don't try to make her vomit at home.

caption:
Diwali's over. If she's still jumping at every sound, still hiding, or still off her food, don't wait for it to wear off.

Fear that outlasts the noise is worth a vet visit. Dogs Trust's advice is to speak to your vet as soon as you see signs of firework fear, and Cats Protection says sooner rather than later. In a Dutch survey of pet parents, more than a third of pets stayed anxious for over half an hour after the fireworks stopped.

New Year's Eve is the next noise night. Booking the visit now gives you weeks, not hours.

PawVeda helps you decide when to see a vet. It doesn't replace one.
